title: The ant's warning
hook: an ant warns the others to hide from Sulayman's army, and he smiles and prays in thanks (27:18–19)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the poets, and your line was words that remember. Whose day did your line of poetry land in? Day five hundred twenty, and a new surah.

People, jinn and birds, all marching in ranks. That's Sulayman's army in Surah An-Naml, the Ant, the twenty-seventh: hosts gathered for him and set in order, moving across the land. And somewhere at ankle height, in a valley, one tiny creature sees it coming. It doesn't run for itself. It turns around and calls to everyone else, before it is too late. The surah is named for that moment, and for that one small voice.
screen: `AN ARMY OF PEOPLE, JINN AND BIRDS.`

segments.voice: Sulayman, the surah says, had been taught the speech of birds. So when the army reaches the Valley of the Ants, he hears this. Pickthall: "O ants! Enter your dwellings lest Solomon and his armies crush you, unperceiving." Notice that last word. The ant doesn't call the army cruel. She says they'll crush us without noticing. She gives a great king the benefit of the doubt, even while she gets everyone out of the way. In Arabic, the ant is feminine, a namla, and the verbs follow. And then the king's reaction. Pickthall: "And (Solomon) smiled, laughing at her speech". No anger, no order to halt and punish. And straight away he turns it into a prayer: my Lord, make me thankful for Your favor on me and my parents, and to do good that pleases Thee. A king hears an insect's voice, and his first words are thanks. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ took the small creatures seriously too. A hadith in Bukhari tells of an earlier prophet, stung by an ant, who had the whole colony burned, and God rebuked him: because one ant stung you, you burned a whole nation that glorified Me? And in Abu Dawud, the Prophet forbade killing four creatures, and the ant is first on the list. The bee, the hoopoe and a small bird of prey are the others. So the story turns the usual picture upside down. The power is all on one side, and the attention, the smile and the thanks go the other way.
screen: `SULAYMAN KNEW THE SPEECH OF BIRDS.` · `CRUSH YOU, UNPERCEIVING.` · `HE SMILED, AND GAVE THANKS.` · `A NATION THAT GLORIFIED ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: step around an ant. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of the smallest living things you share space with: ants on the pavement, a spider in the corner, the birds you never look at. Picture walking out of your door today and seeing a line of ants crossing the path. Picture stopping, watching them for a moment, and stepping around. Notice what it feels like to make yourself slightly less convenient for something tiny. If you pray, you can say Sulayman's words of thanks. The bell holds the time.
The ant's warning. In Surah An-Naml, one ant tells the others to take shelter from Sulayman's army, and the king smiles and gives thanks. Today's word.
Your line: he smiled at the ant. Today, when something small gets in your way, smile at it instead of brushing it aside. Day five hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Muslims recite Sulayman's prayer of thanks from 27:19, and many cite the Prophet's prohibition on killing ants and bees as part of Islamic care for animals.

fork.setup: you're Sulayman, at the head of an army of people, jinn and birds. you hear an ant telling the others to hide from you. what do you do?
options: march on; it's only an ant.
smile, and thank God you heard it.
halt the army and punish the ant.
fork.reveal: he smiled, laughing at her speech, and asked God to make him grateful and to do good that pleases Him.

original.note: Arabic: the ants, the name of surah twenty-seven; one ant is a namla.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cute animal story.
what it means: a king at the head of a vast army hears a tiny voice, and answers with thanks instead of pride.
what a scholar hears: the ant is grammatically feminine, she excuses the army as 'unperceiving', and the hadith of the burned colony in Bukhari sits beside the verse.

sources.quoted: O ants! Enter your dwellings lest Solomon and his armies crush you, unperceiving.

sources.ref: Qur'an 27:16–17 (the speech of birds; the gathered hosts)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3019 (the prophet who burned the ants)
Sunan Abi Dawud 5267 (four creatures not to be killed)

notes: Pickthall 27:18 and the opening of 27:19 quoted from memory; confirm exact wording. The rest of 27:19's prayer is paraphrased.
Bukhari 3019 and Abu Dawud 5267 numbers cited from memory; confirm. The fourth creature (surad) rendered 'a small bird of prey'; translations vary (shrike, sparrow-hawk).

Editor review (2026-10-01): 'Picture' hook opener and unsourced superlatives ('the biggest army anyone has ever marched', 'the most powerful man on earth', 'the greatest army on earth') replaced with the verse's own picture; invented 'the ground shakes' and speculation about Sulayman's feelings cut.
